latin: Posse animam per uiam purgatoriam, absque alio studio uel in/uestigatione, per solam modicam et facillimam collationem et aduertentiam super iam desuper habita intelligibilia, perfectam omnium scibilium scientiam acquirere, non solum Platonici philosophi, sed etiam inter Peripateticos, hi de quibus minus uidetur, Auenrois sequaces habent concedere.

mentions.context: and the Italian Thought of the Renaissance,” in Medieval Aspects of Renaissance Learning: Three Essays, ed. and trans. Edward P. Mahoney (Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1974), 71–3, and Farmer, Syncretism in the West, 47–9 and the notes on 218–31. 8 Conclusions 3>40 (Farmer, 410–11). This passage refers speciﬁcally to acquiring com- plete knowledge through intelligibles above us without relying on inquiry, but by instead following “a purgatorial path” (per uiam purgatoriam). Pico asserts that this position is common to Platonists as well as Aristotelians, though it is “less apparent” in the latter.
